content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new type of distillation loss that encourages the model prediction to be more confident than the teacher. For instance, in the case of binary classification, for positives, make the prediction larger than the teacher label, and for negatives, make the prediction smaller than the teacher label. Various forms of such losses are proposed, such as relational confidence ranking (RCR), which tries to enlarge the prediction distances between two examples, one positive and one negative, or margin-based relational confidence ranking (MRCR), which tries to maximize the margin between two classes of the same example. Experiments on CTR datasets and image classification datasets show superior performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* the paper describes practical industrial setting, and seems to tested with A/B test on real traffic, empirical results seem promising 

weakness
* the idea seems to be somewhat derivative on top of ReLoop.  
* the writing is not very clear, for example, notation is somewhat confusing
  * Eq. (2) is very confusing: what is $\phi$? Is it defined anywhere? is $y$ a function? and you sample $\hat{y}, y_{old}$ from $P(x)$?  
  * notations in Eq. (7) not defined
  * What is $P^+$ and $P^-$? I could guess their meaning, but that’s not right 
  * I understand “CR” is short for confidence ranking, but in experiments, when it refers to CR, I don’t really know which equation of loss it is referring to exactly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* clarity: poor, many notations undefined, many typos, sentences not syntactically correct. 
* quality: fair 
* novelty: fair
* reproducibility: the online experiment on real industrial settings is not reproducible, others seem ok.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposed a new distillation loss to encourage students to have better confidence than the teacher. It’s somewhat incremental to existing work ReLoop. Empirical results seems to show promising results. The writing needs improving and polish. 

some questions: 
* how to tune m in Eq. (5)
* standard setting: “We use the outputs of previous round as input of our proposed method”, you mean in multi-pass training setting, you use the predictions (before back-prop) in last epoch to “teach” in this epoch? 

typos
* space needed before parentheses 
* line after Eq. (10), “ depends one on factor”
* Equation reference no parentheses? a clearer way to refer to equations would be, e.g., Eq. (x)
* “this qualitative bound can still hold majority conditions” -> in majority conditions
* “ KD achieve best accuracy when student is ResNet20 better than CR”

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of continual learning and proposed a new concept named confidence ranking as its solution. The authors rationalized the proposed solution from the perspective of knowledge distillation; and by looking for some ranking-based pairwise surrogate loss to perform the learning. Experiment results were reported on the tasks of click-through rate prediction on three different datasets and a supervised model compression task on CIFAR-100.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is very hard to follow, as it is full of unjustified claims and vague descriptions of the proposed solution. A lot of effort is needed to understand what exactly the proposed solution is. Based on its discussion in the introduction, I believe it is targeting at the continual learning problem; but there is no mentioning about this concept at all, while the authors keep making comparisons against knowledge distillation solutions. To some extend, knowledge distillation could provide a perspective to solve the problem; but these two are not the same problem. Even in the empirical evaluation part, no continual learning baseline was compared at all. In the proposed theoretical analysis, the authors borrowed the conclusion and technique from knowledge distillation; but it is hard to understand why such type of analysis is useful for this clearly continual learning problem.  

On par to the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, the authors proposed a principle/framework named “machine learning application (MLA)”, which really confused me and I am not sure how it compares with ERM.    

The authors argued for the proposed principle of “maximizing the ranking score” as it naturally suits classification tasks in real-world applications and better handles various model complexity. It is really hard to understand these two statements at all. Throughout the paper, the authors kept emphasizing the proposed solution utility confidence of online learnt models for model update, but I really do not see where it quantifies the model’s confidence. Are the authors treating the prediction score as confidence? 

When it comes to the actual disclosure of the proposed method, it seems to me just some regularization term based on two consecutive models’ predictions, which is very standard in continual learning. But the actual description is very hard to decipher again. For example, everything in Section 2.2 depends on the so-called $\phi$-risk, but there is no specification about the $\phi(\cdot)$ function in the paper at all. Is it any loss function we use in practice, or does it require some specific property? In Eq (2), why do we need $y_{old}$ at all? In Eq (3), what is “congruent pair {$x^I, x^{-i}$}”? And why in the first part of Eq (3), we take the difference between $d_f$ and $d_{f_{old}}$ in the $\phi$ function, but in the second part we swap $d_f$ and $d_{f_{old}}$? In Eq (5), what is $m$? And RCR and MRCR only differ in binary classification vs., multi-class classification?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the paper needs to be seriously improved. For example, it is necessary to explicitly explain or define what the intended ranking is and what the key insight of the proposed solution is. The mathematical concepts and notations should be carefully defined and organized such that this part can be self-contained. What’s more, there are numerous grammatical errors, such singular vs., plural form of verbs and nouns, where the authors should pay more attention to address.
content.summary_of_the_review: Neither the proposed solution nor its description was clear enough to deliver the contribution of this work. The described problem sounds like a continual learning problem, but the authors kept connecting it with knowledge distillation. The proposed solution is also standard in continual learning literature, while the paper did not compare with any continual learning methods at all.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to improve the online model performance with the knowledge of previous models. To this end, a distillation-based method is proposed to aggregate the predictions of previous models. The main challenge behind is that the deployed model might be no longer right due to the distribution drift. Inspired by the AUC objective, the authors propose an objective to optimize the ranking between different models. Finally, empirical results on several CTR and classification datasets speak to the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The authors study a practical problem in real-world machine learning systems. To be specific, as the data distribution and online model update rapidly, how to guarantee the online model achieves a satisfactory performance is rather important, especially for some dynamic tasks such as CTR.
- The proposed method is concise and thus easy to follow.
- The empirical results cover two important tasks, which show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Weakness:
- This paper is not well organized. On the one hand, the introduction part is somewhat chaotic and confusing. On the other hand, the motivation of RCR and MRCR are not clarified. Why optimize the output ranking between the current and deployed models could improve the model performance? A more detailed explanation is necessary.
- It seems that the empirical results of MRCR are not satisfactory, which might hinder its application in multiclass problems.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As presented before, the clarity of this paper is somewhat confusing; the proposed methods are concise; the empirical results are sufficient and reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: As presented before, the authors study an important problem, and the proposed method is concise and effective in some empirical results. However, this paper is not well organized and the motivation of the proposed method is not well clarified, which will makes it hard to understand and follow.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper started with a discussion about real-world ML systems where offline training and online learning are combined. A confidence ranking approach is proposed, which tries to make the new model be more confident than the previous model, which is connected to KD. Model compression of image classification problem is also discussed. Experiments are done offline with some public datasets and one internal dataset. The baselines are mostly existing standard CTR prediction or KD methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The paper may have some interesting ideas and potentials to the reviewer.  
Weakness
The writing/organization of the paper is pretty bad unfortunately. The paper is hard to read in general. The interleave between general learning and KD is all over the place and not well organized. The application to model compression in image classification also looks like it is losing focus. Many notations look missing or out of context, e.g., in eq7, the losses are not defined anywhere. It’s hard for the reviewers to understand what is going on. 
It is not clear how the experiments support the claims. The paper started with the offline/online gap in real-world production systems, but the experiments are mostly performed on standard settings and corresponding baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As mentioned, the paper is oblivious to reading right now. It is hard to get the contributions at its current form. 
The reviewer feels the confidence ranking idea might make sense, though I am not convinced it really works as it is not really clearly explained, and the experiments do not seem to support the main claims. The model compression on image classification really looks like a distraction.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper starts with a practical problem setting that discusses offline + online training in production systems. The writing and organization of the paper make it oblivious to understand the novelty and contributions. The experiments do not look directly relevant to the discussed application scenarios. The image classification sections and experiments are distracting.

content.title: Training via Confidence Ranking
content.abstract: Model evolution and constant available data are two common phenomenon in large-scale real-world machine learning application, e.g. ads and recommendation system. To adapt, real-world system typically operates both retraining with all available data and \textit{online-learning} with recent available data to update models periodically with the goal of better serving performance for future data. However, if model and data evolution results in a vastly different training manner, it may induce negative impact on online A/B platform. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, named Confidence Ranking, to design optimization objective as a ranking function with two different models. Our confidence ranking loss allows directly optimizing the logits output for different convex surrogate function of metrics, e.g. AUC and Accuracy depending on the target tasks and datasets. Armed with our proposed methods, our experiments show that the confidence ranking loss can outperform for test-set performance on CTR prediction and model compression with various setting against the knowledge distillation baselines.
